opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is really at the heart of a lot of what goes wrong in how we think about progress in AI. It's essentially Goodhart's law: once a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.

Historically, chess was picked as a benchmark because people believed that playing chess well *required* general intelligence. The reasoning was: humans who are great at chess seem to be very smart, they plan, they reason abstractly, they model their opponent, so if a machine can do it, it must have those capabilities too. Chess was a proxy, a measure of something deeper we actually cared about.

But the moment the community turned it into the target, the question became "how do we beat the world champion?" rather than "how do we build systems that reason the way we hoped chess would reveal?" And it turns out there are shortcuts. You can exploit the specific structure of the game: perfect information, a fixed rule set, a tractable simulator, and enormous compute for search. Deep Blue was an incredible engineering achievement, but it didn't tell us much about general intelligence. It told us that chess can be solved, to a superhuman level, by methods that don't transfer to most of the problems we care about.

And I think that's a pattern we keep repeating. Go was the next version of it. Atari, StarCraft, and now a lot of the language benchmarks. Each time, we optimize for the number, the number goes up, and then we realize the number was capturing a much narrower thing than we thought.

So for me the lesson isn't that games are bad. I love games as research environments, and a lot of my own work is on multi-agent settings like Hanabi, precisely because they force you to deal with things like theory of mind and coordination with others. The lesson is that you have to be really clear about *why* you're using an environment. What is the capability you're trying to probe? And then you should be suspicious of your own successes. If you solve it, ask: did I get the capability, or did I find the shortcut?

One practical consequence is that we should care much more about generalization: held-out partners, held-out conditions, ad-hoc teamwork, zero-shot coordination. That's much harder to Goodhart, because you can't simply overfit to the one thing you're evaluated on. If a method only works on the benchmark it was tuned on, that's a strong signal you've been treating the measure as a target.

r001.rationale: The response does not say chess as a measure requires limiting learning to a human-comparable number of samples.

r002.rationale: It says chess as a target can be solved through shortcuts and enormous compute for search, but does not clearly identify brute force as substituting for imaginative problem-solving.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most important distinctions in the whole history of the field, and chess is the cleanest example of it. If you go back to the early days, people like Turing and Shannon and so on picked chess because it seemed like a proxy for intelligence. The reasoning was: humans who are good at chess are generally smart, chess requires planning, reasoning, abstraction, pattern recognition, all these things we associate with intelligence. So the idea was, if we can build a machine that plays chess well, we must have captured something fundamental about intelligence. Chess was a measure, a thermometer, if you like.

And then what happened is the classic Goodhart story. The moment you make chess the target, the moment the goal becomes "beat the world champion," the field optimises directly for that, and you end up with Deep Blue. Deep Blue is an incredible engineering achievement, but it's essentially brute-force search plus a hand-crafted evaluation function. It beats Kasparov, and then everyone goes, hang on, this thing is not intelligent in any general sense. It can't play checkers, it can't tie its shoes, it has nothing to say about anything else. So the measure got decoupled from the thing it was supposed to measure, precisely because we targeted it.

I think there's a real lesson there for how we do research today. When something is a measure, it has to be a bit incidental. You develop a general method for some other reason, and then you say, okay, let's check, does this general method also happen to play chess? That's informative. AlphaZero is actually much closer to that spirit, because the same algorithm plays chess, Go, and shogi without being told anything about those games specifically. The chess result tells you something about the method, not just about chess.

But the moment the community agrees that a benchmark is the thing to beat, and leaderboards go up, and papers get accepted or rejected based on it, the benchmark stops being a measure. People start building in domain-specific tricks, tuning hyperparameters on the test distribution, essentially overfitting the entire research community to the benchmark. And then you get this surprised reaction every few years where someone says, we solved the benchmark but the capability didn't generalise.

So my take is, you need both, but you have to be very honest about which one you're doing. Targets are fine for engineering, for driving progress on a specific capability. But if you want to make claims about intelligence or general capabilities, you need measures that you are deliberately not optimising for, ideally ones the method has never seen. And that's actually hard, because the incentive structure in the field constantly pushes you to turn every measure into a target.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that measuring AI with chess requires limiting learning to a human-comparable number of samples.

r002.rationale: It says targeting chess led to Deep Blue’s brute-force search and did not demonstrate general intelligence, but it does not connect this substitution to imaginative problem-solving.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s an important distinction between asking, “Can our AI play chess?” and saying, “Let’s build an AI to play chess.” If chess is a measure, you’re using it to probe capabilities that you hope are more general: planning, reasoning, making decisions. If chess is the target, you can put all your effort into exploiting the particular structure of that game.

And that’s perfectly legitimate, but it changes what you can conclude from success. A system that plays excellent chess has demonstrated excellent chess play. Whether it tells us something broader about intelligence depends on how it got there, what assumptions we built in, and whether those capabilities transfer to other problems.

The danger is that we start with chess as a proxy for something we care about, then optimize the proxy so heavily that we lose sight of the original question.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes chess as a capability probe from chess as a target, but does not state that learning must be limited to a human-comparable number of samples.

r002.rationale: It says a chess target permits effort focused on exploiting the game's structure, but does not say computational brute force substitutes for imaginative problem-solving.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s an important distinction between using chess to measure progress towards something more general and making chess itself the objective. As a measure, it can be useful: it’s a well-defined problem, and you can compare systems quite cleanly. But once it becomes the target, you start selecting for whatever makes a system better at chess, and that doesn’t necessarily tell you much about intelligence more broadly.

You might develop ideas that transfer, or you might become exceptionally good at exploiting the structure of that particular game. The score alone doesn’t distinguish those possibilities. So the question is: what did we actually want chess to tell us, and does improving at chess still provide evidence for that?

r001.rationale: The response calls chess a well-defined, comparable measure but says nothing about limiting learning to a human-comparable number of samples.

r002.rationale: It notes that optimizing for chess can exploit the game's structure, but does not state that computational brute force can substitute for imaginative problem-solving.
